## Exploratory data analysis

Data are from: Mesquita, Daniel O., et al. “Life history data of lizards of the world (Ecological Archives E096-058).” Ecology 96.2 (2015): 594-594.

Looks like there are lots of NAs in our data, particularly in the measured observation. Reproduction, foraging, distribution, and habitat all have lots of data. Of measured data, also mean clutch siz, clutch frequency, and mean.f.svl
*What's the difference between clutch frequency and clutch number per year? frequency has many more observations, but the numbers are quite similar. 

```{r looking at trends}
#read in dataset
lizard <- read.csv("lizard.csv")

head(lizard)
dim(lizard)
tail(lizard) #oooh empty rows i hate that, let's delete
names(lizard)
str(lizard)

#then let's look at NAs - lots!
colSums(is.na(lizard))

#let's look at what we do know, to try to choose a balanced design
table(lizard$Family)
table(lizard$Mode.of.reproduction) #lots, but not balanced
table(lizard$Foraging.Mode) #well balanced!
table(lizard$Distribution) #also well balanced!
table(lizard$Prefered.Habitat.Type) #not well balanced at all, beware
summary(lizard$Mean.Clutch.Size) #huh. probably a few high outliers. only 4 NAs
table(lizard$Clutch.Frequency) #weird low outliers, probably. i bet this might match with eggs v living. plot it!
```

```{r cleaning data}
#ok first let's remove the empty rows at the end
lizard <- lizard[1:(nrow(lizard)-3), ]

#now let's change our variables to be numeric, where they should be
lizard %>%
  mutate(SD.Female.adult.weight..g. = as.numeric(SD.Female.adult.weight..g.)) -> lizard


```

## Visualizing


```{r intro visualizing}
hist(lizard$Mean.Clutch.Size)
hist(lizard$Clutch.Frequency)
hist(lizard$Mean.F.SVL.adults..mm.)

#to see relationship of repro mode and clutch size. not as obvious as i thought
ggplot(lizard, aes(x = Mode.of.reproduction,
                   y = Mean.Clutch.Size,
                   fill = Mode.of.reproduction)) + geom_boxplot()

ggplot(lizard, aes(x = Prefered.Habitat.Type,
                   y = Mean.Clutch.Size,
                   fill = Distribution)) + geom_boxplot()

```
Let's look at a pca to see if we can get at explaining family from some of these numerical stats
```{r exploratory PCAs}
#first, looking again at families
sort(table(lizard$Family), decreasing = TRUE) -> family_counts #plenty here with very few individuals, so let's cut our dataset down to....the top 12

top12_families <- names(family_counts)[1:12]

lizard_top12 <- lizard[lizard$Family %in% top12_families,]

table(lizard_top12$Family)

#ok, then, looking at which numerical variables we have...
str(lizard_top12)

#we should choose those we're interested in, that have the fewest NAs
lizard_top12 %>%
  select(
    Mean.F.SVL.adults..mm.,
    F.SVL.at.maturity..mm.,
    Mean.Clutch.Size,
    Clutch.Frequency) %>%
  na.omit() %>%
  scale() %>%
  as.data.frame() -> lizard_scaled

PCA(lizard_scaled, 
    scale.unit = TRUE, # Option to center and scale data (useless here)
    ncp = 4, # Number of components to keep (here, all)
    graph = FALSE) -> pca_lizard

summary(pca_lizard)

fviz_eig(pca_lizard, choice = "variance")

fviz_pca_var(pca_lizard,
             axes = c(1, 2), col.var="cos2")
```
```{r random forest}
lizard_top12 %>%
  select(
    Family,
    Mean.F.SVL.adults..mm.,
    F.SVL.at.maturity..mm.,
    Mean.Clutch.Size,
    Clutch.Frequency) %>%
  na.omit() -> rf_lizard

# Check how many observations remain after removing NAs
nrow(rf_lizard)

#make a dataset with quant and qual
forest_vars <- c(
  "Mean.F.SVL.adults..mm.",
  "F.SVL.at.maturity..mm.",
  "Offspring.SVL..mm.",
  "Mean.Clutch.Size",
  "Clutch.Frequency",
  "Mode.of.reproduction",
  "Distribution",
  "Foraging.Mode",
  "Prefered.Habitat.Type")

# Check missing values in each predictor
colSums(is.na(lizard_top12[, forest_vars]))

# Count how many rows have complete data for all predictors
sum(complete.cases(lizard_top12[, c("Family", forest_vars)]))

forest_data <- lizard_top12 %>%
  select(Family, all_of(forest_vars)) %>%
  na.omit() %>%
  mutate(across(where(is.character), as.factor))

# Check how many observations remain
nrow(forest_data)

# Check how many observations there are in each family
table(forest_data$Family)

#here we go!
set.seed(123)

split_lizard <- initial_split(forest_data, prop = 0.75, strata = "Family") #this allows us to split our dataset into training and testing datasets
train_lizard <- analysis(split_lizard)
test_lizard  <- assessment(split_lizard)

# Check the sizes
dim(train_lizard)
nrow(test_lizard)

# Check family representation in each set
table(train_lizard$Family)
table(test_lizard$Family)

forest <- randomForest(
  Family ~ .,
  data = train_lizard,
  ntree = 1000, 
  importance = TRUE)

forest_predictions <- predict(forest, newdata = select(test_lizard, -Family))

forest_confusion <- confusionMatrix(forest_predictions, test_lizard$Family) 
forest_confusion

varImpPlot(forest)

```
